findings.claim: Bar: published plugin installed by strangers (addendum ~L100); portability ranks second (~L114). The note's path breaks the operator's 'it ships' ruling. install.sh copies only skill/ and agents/. FC4 also classes every `docs/…` reference as a target-project file and skips it. A lens that cites `docs/process-constants.md` passes CI green, then resolves in the user's repo, where the file does not exist. Of the three homes: (a) a new chorus-core reference file beside ROSTER.md/BINDINGS.md keeps dependency direction (everyone already composes core). It costs a non-mechanical file in the substrate and one index line in SKILL.md. (b) A section of CONDUCTOR.md puts advisory prose inside the file that holds the binding I1-I9 catalog. That makes it harder to tell what binds and what advises, and every conductor read gets heavier. (c) chorus-learn inverts the direction: review, sdlc and the personas would depend on a tutorial that only composes core.

findings.claim: C1-C9 is a fourth id family next to I/S/D. Calling it advisory does not exempt it. The failure is not an obligation nobody meets. It is an id that gets redefined or forks once ten personas start citing it, which is contract coupling on a bare token. FC1 defines and resolves only the I, D and S families. No C-token appears in skill/ or agents/ today, so the check is cheap to add before the first caller. Ruling: single home in the new core file, plus an FC1 extension. Definitions anywhere else fail the build, and a cited Cn with no definition fails as a dangling token. Cost: one loop and one regex. Payoff: conformance, ranked first.

findings.claim: Duplicate-authority ruling: CONSOLIDATE, with direction stated. Even as rationale, the bullets restate rules the canon owns: the named owner who closes validation is I9, and ranking and asked-once rulings are D/S mechanics. findings.claim: Ruling 1 says the note ships, but at docs/process-constants.md it cannot. install.sh only copies skill/*/ and agents/, so the file never reaches a copy install. A lens that cites `docs/process-constants.md` passes CI, because § 4a classes docs/… and lower-case names as target-project files and never checks them. At run time that path resolves into the user's own repo, where the file does not exist. Once the note moves into skill/chorus-core/, the release path costs almost nothing. The installer loop picks the file up, the manifest covers uninstall with no orphans, roundtrip line 73 already compares every installed file to its source, and check 4c forces an entry in the SKILL.md index. The one choice that matters is the name. An upper-case bare name (PROCESS-CONSTANTS.md) is resolved and checked by § 4a against the citing directory and then chorus-core. findings.claim: Implication 4 tells the next round to put a recurring finding's workaround 'where the next round reads it' but names no place, and under ruling 4 no store exists. Shipping that advice has a running cost. Each lens that follows it will pick its own spot, such as persona memory, a round record or a brief ruling. Persona memory is excluded from review, and past records are never rewritten (addendum § 2). The known errors would end up scattered across stores that nobody reviews and that drift apart. That is the opposite of a KEDB. The cheapest honest fix is one sentence that points at the surface that already exists, the Gate upkeep procedure in EXPLORATORY-PHASE.md, or that says plainly that chorus does not keep a known-error store yet.

findings.claim: Installs pick up a new version of the note when install.sh is re-run. A copy the user edited is kept as 'differs, kept', and nothing else announces the change. A lens cannot tell which version of the note it read. The run log stamps only the VERSION string in the header (conduct.mjs:712), and no rule says when VERSION must be bumped. Bumping it for a wording change has a cost: every in-flight run log refuses to resume (ENGINE_MISMATCH). At one maintainer the cheapest contract is to cite by ID and keep the IDs stable. C1–C9 are append-only, a retired constant is struck out and its number is never reused, and the note states this rule in one line. Then a citation of 'C7' in an old record stays true across versions without a VERSION bump.

findings.claim: Most ops claims hold. The ITIL incident/problem split, the KEDB, proactive problem management and the lineage of CD from PDSA are accurate. One claim overreaches. That is survey correlation about external approval, not proof that a CAB 'doesn't improve stability', and DORA found lightweight peer review helpful. Name the source, say 'heavyweight external', and use 'no evidence it improves'. The KEDB-for-agents claim at :63 is reasoning without data. Label it as inference.

findings.claim: Once the note ships, any lens can cite a C-id as [principle] evidence ('existing; cite where established'). I8 then passes a finding whose only grounding is 'C1'. The lens benefits: it gets evidence without tracing an artefact chain. The operator pays: they get a finding they cannot check against their own code, plus an opaque id they must look up in an installed skill folder. The operator ruled the note advisory (ruling 2), and the note says it is not binding. But nothing stops it being used as evidence, and that use is what makes it binding in practice. Fix it in the same change: state in the note, and once in BRIEFS item 8, that a C-id is rationale and never evidence. Always write it with its name ('C1 attention'), never as a bare id. findings.claim: The difference between verification and validation exists only in the note's prose. In lifecycle mode the operator sees 'Gate C clears' and then a 'sign-off', which is only a memory update (sdlc-log.schema.json:134). Together they read as 'goal reached'. No field or label in the record says 'verified; validation open, closed by <operator>'. The operator forms the belief 'validated' from a signal that means 'verified', which leaves a gulf of evaluation open. The operator ruled 'show it in the record'. The record, or its rendering, should state that validation is still open and name who closes it. Review mode has the same gap (see F6). This is a schema or renderer change, separate from relocating the note.

findings.claim: Line 85 says 'DORA found CAB approval doesn't improve stability'. That is broader than the source. DORA's capability page (fetched by Norman on 2026-11-06) reports survey correlation: it found 'no evidence' that a more formal, external review process was associated with lower change-fail rates, and it found heavyweight approaches lead to larger, less frequent batches. The same page cites the 2019 State of DevOps Report recommending peer review during development supplemented by automation. The other ITIL claims hold (incident/problem split, KEDB, proactive problem management). The fix is to cite the page and narrow the wording, for example: 'DORA found no evidence that formal external change approval lowers change-fail rates, and it slows delivery into larger batches; peer review plus automation is the surviving form.' The claim at line 63 that a known-error list matters more with agents is reasoning without data; label it as inference.
